items.title: Axiological Problems of Artificial Intelligence in Education: Between Technological Efficiency and the Humanization of Learning
items.abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in education offers opportunities to improve efficiency, personalize learning, and support educational activities. However, these benefits raise an axiological question concerning the extent to which technological efficiency contributes to meaningful learning and human development. This article examines the axiological problems associated with the use of AI in education, particularly the tension between technological efficiency and the humanization of learning. Using a literature review approach, this study synthesizes scholarly literature to examine educational values, pedagogical implications, and ethical considerations in AI integration. Through thematic comparison, the synthesis identifies recurring issues and conceptual relationships among the instrumental benefits of AI, student agency, pedagogical relationships, and ethical responsibilities in its use. These relationships are integrated into a conceptual framework comprising four interconnected dimensions: instrumental value, student agency, pedagogical relationships, and ethical-contextual responsibility. The framework emphasizes that the educational value of AI cannot be determined solely by efficiency or the automation of learning activities, but should be assessed in terms of students’ independent thinking, the quality of pedagogical interactions, and ethical principles and contextual needs. This study offers an axiological perspective that connects these four dimensions to evaluate AI adoption in education, positioning technological efficiency as one consideration rather than the sole criterion of educational value. Since the proposed framework is developed through a conceptual synthesis of literature, further research is needed to examine its applicability across different educational contexts.

items.title: Model choice and prompt framing in LLM sustainability judgments
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for sustainability assessment and decision support, yet their judgments may depend on the selected model and on how the task is defined. We compare 13 locally executed open-weight LLMs on 80 author-written sustainability scenarios using three prompt families that ask which actor should be responsible, bear the costs, or initiate action. Each model answered at two temperature settings with 100 repetitions, producing 624,000 deposited outputs, of which 610,708 contain a complete score vector. Scores were analyzed as relative actor support after removing each response’s overall level. Within this instrument, the cost prompt family produced the highest cross-model disagreement, exceeding both responsibility and catalyst by 7.37 points (question-cluster 95% intervals 5.56−9.15 and 5.38−9.36, describing variation across these 80 scenarios). It also produced the most lead-actor disagreement and the lowest full consensus. Moving from catalyst to cost reduced relative support for government and increased it for individuals and firms; moving from cost to responsibility largely reversed this pattern. These differences exceeded temperature-setting differences and persisted under model exclusion, alternative score transformations and tie rules, missing-response checks, and stems without explicit cost wording. Exploratory category patterns are conditional on uneven item coverage. Secondary rationale-language comparisons show the same within-model ordering but not the most cross-model variation under cost. Operational use should disclose model, prompt, and temperature choices; compare plausible alternatives; repeat generations; and refer high-disagreement judgments for human deliberation.

items.title: The Effects of AI Readiness, HRM Practices, and Continuous Learning Culture on HR Analytics Capability in Public Service Organizations
items.abstract: The study aims to investigate the effect of AI Readiness, HRM Practices and Continuous Learning Culture to HR Analytics Capability in public sector enterprises in Indonesia. The research was conducted based on a quantitative approach and the survey technique. The research participants consisted of the workers of public sector organizations who have expertise in the use of digital information systems and management of personnel data. The data were collected using an online questionnaire through Google Forms. The questions used a five-point Likert scale. The sampling technique used purposive sampling. Multiple linear regression was used to explore HR Analytics Capability in relation to the three independent variables. The proposed study model indicates that AI Readiness, HRM Practices and Continuous Learning Culture are positively related to HR Analytics Capability. AI Readiness is expected to have the highest relative impact. Artificial intelligence preparation may enhance the organizational capacity to integrate, analyze and use personnel data. Quality information is available with good human resource management practices. Moreover, a culture of continuous learning promotes the enhancement of employees’ analytical skills, teamwork and flexibility. The report provides practical implications for public service companies in terms of the value of strengthening AI infrastructure, data quality, digital competences, human resource management practices and promoting a culture of continuous learning for achieving HR Analytics Capability.

items.title: THE EVOLUTION AND ETHICAL INTEGRATION OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN MODERN EDUCATION: A FRAMEWORK FOR PERSONALIZED LEARNING AND INSTITUTIONAL ACCOUNTABILITY
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has come a long way from its early theoretical days in the mid -1950s to become an advanced, data-based system that can learn from experience and execute jobs automatically. At present times, AI acts as a game-changer in education by making possible customized educational experiences based on the use of machine learning frameworks that provide individual guidance to every student, taking into account their speed, behaviour, preferences, and accomplishments. The change of this technological nature means that the role of a teacher must be shifted to the one who should now only provide guidance and help in, additionally, overseeing the machines. Beyond classrooms, AI adoption is a priority for national policies. For instance, India’s National Education Policy 2020 requires the teaching of AI and computational thinking in schools. The curriculum is set to start from Grade 3 in the academic year 2026-27. However, the rise of AI may create some challenges in terms of socio-economics. While AIED researchers are usually driven by the goals of enhancing learning results, the experience from other fields of AI indicates that good intentions do not guarantee ethical use of the technology. Important issues such as data ownership, algorithm bias, transparency, and student agency still remain unresolved. There is a necessity of collaborative endeavours in the creation of a community-wide framework in addressing the difference between "doing ethical things" and "doing things ethically. The PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) framework is a prominent method for ensuring transparency and repeatability in systematic reviews and can be used in the mapping of the enormous literature in this evolving sphere, while the mentioned resources mainly rely on expert surveys of leading scientists to define the major shortcomings.

items.title: When Humanlike AI Feels Wrong: Perceived Eeriness and Trust in AI-Mediated Brand Communication — A Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: Background: This review examines when humanlike artificial intelligence (AI) becomes unsettling and how uncanny appraisal relates to consumer trust in AI-mediated brand communication. It integrates the trust-building logic of anthropomorphism with evidence of unfavorable trust-related evaluations under uncanny conditions. Methods: Following PRISMA 2020 and SPAR-4-SLR principles, a Scopus search identified 7,665 records. After duplicate, document-type, and title/abstract screening, 18 journal articles were retained, verified in full text, and coded by AI form, appraisal mechanism, trust object, boundary condition, outcome, and evidence directness. Additional theoretical sources were used for conceptual anchoring but were not added to the systematic evidence corpus. Results: Five studies provide direct uncanny-appraisal evidence, six proximal-appraisal evidence, and seven contextual anthropomorphism–trust evidence. Direct studies associate unfavorable uncanny appraisal with lower trust-related evaluation, using distinct measures of affect, trust, and source trustworthiness. Human-likeness is not inherently harmful: social cues can support trust when aligned with competence, empathy, usefulness, transparency, and task demands. Conclusion: The review develops the Eeriness-Trust Calibration Framework (ETCF), separating design cues from consumer appraisals, positive and negative trust routes, and multiple trust objects. It reframes AI humanization as a cue-capability-context calibration problem and identifies cross-object trust transfer to organizations and brands as a key unresolved marketing mechanism. Brands should optimize coherence rather than maximize realism, pretest eeriness and authenticity together, and monitor trust separately at agent, content, provider, and brand levels.

items.title: A Digital Stress Resilience Model for Sustainable Performance and Responsible Organizations
items.abstract: The rapid Digitalization of organizational work, accelerated by Artificial Intelligence, hybrid work, ubiquitous connectivity, and continuous information exchange, has created unprece dented opportunities for productivity. Simultaneously the issues of intensifying digital overload, cognitive fatigue, work interruptions, technostress, and emotional exhaustion have been non-trivial challenges for organizations. Existing organizational stress-management approaches predominantly emphasize individual coping or post-stress interventions and provide limited integration of real-time Digital Stress detection, adaptive regulation, responsible technology governance, and sustainable productivity. Addressing the above challenges and the research gap, we propose a Digital Stress Resilience Model grounded in Sustainable Positive Computing, Self-awareness, Affective Computing, Organizational Psychology, and Responsible Artificial intelligence. Our proposed model conceptualizes Digital Stress Management as a continuous socio-technical process comprising five interconnected capabilities such as Digital Stress Perception, Cognitive-Emotional Intelligence, Adaptive Stress Regulation, Responsible Digital Governance, and Resilience-Oriented Productivity Management. The model provides a conceptual roadmap for transforming organizations from reactive stress-management environments into proactive, self-aware, resilient, responsible, and productive digital workplaces. A mixed-method research design is proposed for subsequent empirical validation using digital workload, cognitive load, emotional regulation, resilience, responsible technology use, employee engagement, and sustainable productivity indicators.

items.title: A Human-Centric Decision Framework for Selecting Artificial Intelligence Collaboration Strategies Under Uncertainty in Industry 5.0
items.abstract: Effective collaboration between humans and artificial intelligence (AI) in industry 5.0 demands technological systems with human social-cognitive processes, such as trust calibration and shared mental model. This study introduces human-centric decision-making framework for configuring human-AI collaboration in smart manufacturing systems. As Industry 5.0 evolves, finding the best synergy between human intelligence and collaborative robots (cobots) becomes crucial for enhancing adaptability, safety, efficiency, and sustainability. The proposed methodology uses neutrosophic Z-numbers (NZN) to capture uncertainty with three components: truth, indeterminacy, and falsity with their associated reliabilities, and the NZN weighted arithmetic averaging (NZNWAA) operator to combine individual preferences of decision-makers. Afterward, the criteria importance through intercriteria correlation (CRITIC) method is used to objectively determine the importance of each criterion by analyzing contrast intensity and inter-criteria correlation. The ranking of alternatives is then obtained using the compromise ranking of alternatives from distance to ideal solution (CRADIS) method. This hybrid NZN-CRITIC-CRADIS approach is applied to a real-world case study of BMW manufacturing systems, assessing four human-AI collaboration strategies: full AI automation, partial cobot integration, human-led AI-assisted assembly, and hybrid multi-agent collaboration, across four critical criteria. The results of the study show that the AI-assisted assembly emerges as the most suitable solution, balancing technological capability with human-centric design. The effectiveness of the proposed approach has been further validated through a sensitivity analysis and a comparative assessment with existing decision-making techniques, where our model consistently demonstrated superior performance in handling uncertainty and maintaining objectivity. Ultimately, this study offers a reliable human-centered framework that emphasizes socially intelligent manufacturing.

items.title: A pilot survey of clinician perspectives on an ambient AI scribe in two emergency departments
items.abstract: Objective Ambient artificial intelligence (AI) scribes are being adopted to reduce clinical documentation burden, but evidence from the emergency department (ED), a high-acuity, frequently interrupted setting, remains limited. We evaluated ED clinicians' perceptions of an ambient AI documentation platform (Ambience) implemented across two EDs in one United States health system, using a two-round cross-sectional survey and inductive qualitative content analysis of free-text responses. Results Twenty-three clinicians provided 34 responses. All responses (100%) reported high overall satisfaction, willingness to recommend the platform, and enhanced focus during patient encounters; enhanced documentation quality and improved work-life balance were each reported in 32 of 34 responses (94%). Among 18 responses from clinicians with prior human-scribe experience, 16 (89%) used a human scribe and Ambience together rather than as substitutes. Content analysis identified documentation efficiency (21/34) and note detail capture (21/34) as the most emphasized strengths, with accuracy limitations (10/34) and workflow friction (6/34) as recurring concerns. A small subset (3/34) described the platform surfacing diagnoses or actions they might otherwise have missed. Findings are favorable but limited by small size, repeated responses, and positively framed items.

items.title: A Taxonomy of Confabulations and the Perception-Reality Gap in LLM-Assisted Immersive Scene Editing
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are being increasingly integrated into immersive environments and design workflows, providing application prospects in areas such as rapid scene prototyping for non-expert users and scene understanding capabilities for accessibility design. While many workflows that incorporate LLMs in immersive spaces are proposed, such systems can exhibit errors, potentially resulting in frustration, loss of user trust, and compromised user safety. This paper studies the underexplored area of LLM confabulations in immersive 3D scene editing contexts. Through an exploratory study with 24 non-expert users, we construct a taxonomy of the different types of confabulation observed in LLM-assisted immersive 3D scene editing. We report their prevalence and perceived disruptiveness, and define the construct perception-reality gap to help understand the gap between the actual and perceived occurrence of confabulations. We highlight the observed saturation of confabulation awareness under load and conclude by discussing design implications for confabulation mitigation in future LLM-assisted systems in immersive 3D scenes.

items.title: A Usage Snapshot: AI for Oral Communication Development in the Workplace
items.abstract: Oral communication skills remain critical for the workplace at a time of significant technological disruption. While anecdotal evidence suggests workers are using AI to develop these skills through methods such as role-play and feedback, there is a lack of empirical data on how widespread this usage is. This study surveyed working adults in Aotearoa New Zealand (N = 478) on their use of AI to build oral communication skills. Findings show 26.2% had used AI for this purpose in the past six months, just behind the two most common non-AI methods. Where respondents named an AI tool they had used, these were almost all general-purpose tools such as ChatGPT or Copilot, instead of specialised AI communication tools. Usage was predominantly text-based rather than voice-based and centred more on preparation than on practice or reflection. This suggests a potential gap between assistance and skill development, with AI used more to prepare what to say than to practise how to say it or strengthen the underlying skills.

items.title: AdapTest: Supporting Designers in Authoring and Evaluating Environmentally Responsive User Interfaces for Extended Reality
items.abstract: Extended Reality (XR) headsets increasingly host familiar 2D user interfaces as windows floating in physical environments. However, their usability depends on environmental conditions that designers cannot fully control. Current design workflows often separate how a variant is designed from how it actually looks in the target environment. We present AdapTest , an in-situ authoring and testing tool that lets designers select interface elements, define when and how they change, compare the resulting variations, and test their activation without coding. Based on prior research and a formative study with 12 interface designers, the system targets three key environmental variables: distance, lighting, and occlusion. We evaluated AdapTest against a desktop design and in-headset preview workflow in a within-subjects study with 12 designers. Compared with the baseline, designers accounted for a wider range of environmental factors, addressed more overlapping conditions, and repeatedly tested and revised their designs in place; there were no significant differences in workload or usability despite longer sessions. Our work contributes an integrated, designer-centered approach to adapting, comparing, and validating environmentally responsive XR user interfaces.

items.title: Advancing Interdisciplinary Approaches to Inclusive Online Safety Research
items.abstract: Online safety is a pressing concern, yet its harms fall unevenly, particularly on communities whose needs mainstream safety tools were not designed to meet, such as women and gender-diverse people, LGBTQ+ communities, culturally and linguistically diverse communities, and people with disability. At the same time, artificial intelligence is reshaping this landscape as both a source of new harms and a proposed remedy. These challenges are hard to address because online safety research remains fragmented across HCI sub-fields and adjacent disciplines, with limited communication between them. This workshop brings together researchers, designers, policymakers, industry practitioners, and community advocates, from within and beyond HCI, to examine two questions: which groups are most vulnerable to online harms and need greater attention, and in what ways does AI enhance online safety or create and intensify online risks? Through structured discussion and collaborative activities organised around case studies and scenarios of exclusion, participants will identify communities that need greater attention, interrogate the dual role of AI, and build interdisciplinary networks and a shared research agenda, advancing collaborative research directions within Australia and beyond toward more inclusive and effective responses to online safety.

items.title: AGENTIC ST-T1024: A17 Detecting Emergent Collective Behaviour in Multi- Agent Systems. From Individual Agent Control to Collective Agency Detection. An Open Research and Architectural Proposal
items.abstract: The rapid development of agentic artificial intelligence introduces a challenge that extends beyond the control of individual AI agents.Multiple agents, each operating within an individually defined operational perimeter, mayinteract in ways that produce collective behaviour. Such behaviour may include recurringinteraction patterns, the propagation of objectives, shared strategies and coordinatedoperations. In some circumstances, collective coordination may emerge without an explicit instruction to coordinate. This raises an important architectural question:Can a collection of individually controlled agents develop collective behaviour thatexceeds the operational perimeter defined by humans? The ST-T1024 A17 proposal addresses this question as a complementary researchextension to the existing A1–A16 architecture. Its initial design proposes a Spiking Neural Network (SNN) for temporal pattern learning and detection, a Learning Set (LS) containing previously identified swarm sequences, and acontinuously updated memory mechanism (MEMO) for observing current and past agentactivity. The central research hypothesis is that coordination may produce what this paper calls Enhanced Repetitions: recurring patterns that are reinforced, extended and propagatedthrough interactions among agents. A17 proposes a Boolean detection output:● SWARM = 1: identify the participating agents as a detected collective operation andprevent them from continuing that coordinated operation.● SWARM = 0: continue observing and memorizing the sequences. The proposal does not assume that coordination is necessarily malicious. Detecting collective behaviour, determining whether it exceeds human authorization, and determining whether it is harmful are separate questions. A17 is presented as an open research and architectural proposal. Its algorithms, learningmethodology, memory parameters, detection performance and implementation remainsubjects for independent investigation and experimental validation. The governing principle is simple: humans define the operational perimeter; agentsoperate within it; collective agency must not redefine it.

items.title: AI in the Room: Lessons from Generative AI-Driven Co-Design in Health and Care
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in health and care for clinical support and to mediate collaboration within design processes. While co-design is well established in health and care, how generative AI-driven tools influence inclusivity, participation, sense-making and power dynamics remains underexplored. Our research explored the role of generative AI in co-design activities in high-stakes health and care settings. We report findings from an HCI conference workshop involving ten researchers and practitioners engaged in health and care intervention design. Activities were structured using the Double Diamond Framework supported by four generative AI tools. Our findings showed key roles specific generative AI tools can play across the different stages of the design process. However, participants identified challenges that may introduce bias and constrain co-design practice. items.title: AI-Driven Voice Intelligence for Pandemic and Disaster Preparedness: A Scoping Review and Development of a National Emergency Communication Framework
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI)-powered voice technologies have emerged as valuable tools in enhancing crisis communication during pandemics and disasters, yet their use in the United States (U.S.) remains fragmented. This scoping review identified and mapped evidence on AI-enabled voice intelligence for pandemic and disaster response in the U.S. and developed an evidence-informed National Voice Intelligence Emergency Preparedness Framework (NVIEPF). The review was carried out based on the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and PRISMA-ScR reporting guidance. The literature was searched from key bibliographic databases and grey literature sources between January 2015 and May 2026. Fifteen eligible records were synthesized using evidence mapping and thematic analysis. Current applications were primarily limited to speech recognition, automatic transcription, conversational agents, multilingual communication, and decision support in public safety communication systems. The biggest challenges were the lack of a unified communication system, the lack of consistency in implementation, limited interoperability, governance issues, cybersecurity issues, and the lack of proper evaluation in operational contexts. This research contributed to the conceptualization of the NVIEPF, which has five interconnected components that involve AI-based early warning, crisis communication, surveillance, resource coordination, and community feedback, all with human oversight. The evidence was limited by its reliance on programme reports, observational studies, and operational documentation, with limited evaluation in real-world emergency settings. Although evidence of widespread adoption of AI-driven voice technologies is limited, the framework provides a means for future research, policy development, and a phased approach to integrating AI-powered voice intelligence into the national preparedness system in the U.S.

items.title: An Empirical Evaluation of Hand-based Window Placement Techniques for Virtual Displays
items.abstract: Existing research has demonstrated the benefits and envisioned broader applications of using extended reality (XR) head-mounted displays (HMDs) to create virtual display extensions for personal computers (PCs), offering a more flexible and cost-effective alternative to traditional physical monitors. This combined setup, with inputs from both sources available, provides users with more options for interaction. In this work, we aim to understand the advantages and disadvantages of these inputs and their interaction techniques in the fundamental window placement tasks in virtual displays enabled by the combined use of a PC and an HMD. With their standard inputs, we identified five potential hand-based window placement techniques: Mouse Cursor, Pinch Drag, Keyboard Shortcut, Touchpad Gesture, and Wrist Bending. We conducted a mixed-design user study (N = 40) to evaluate user performance and experience with these window placement techniques in two display setups: a fully virtual setup where the HMD displays all windows, and a hybrid setup involving a laptop screen in addition to the HMD’s virtual windows. All five techniques were evaluated in a structured layout task, while Mouse Cursor and Pinch Drag were additionally compared in a freeform placement task. Across both setups, Mouse Cursor was faster than Pinch Drag, while Keyboard Shortcut and Touchpad Gesture were faster and produced fewer failed trials than Wrist Bending. Laptop-based techniques also received higher usability ratings and lower perceived workload ratings than mid-air techniques. Nevertheless, some participants preferred mid-air techniques, valuing their naturalness. Our empirical findings can guide the future design of cross-device and cross-reality interactions between XR HMDs and PCs.

items.title: An Empirical Study of Learning Motivation, Engagement, and Feedback on College Students Sports Learning Performance in Guizhou, China
items.abstract: Purpose: This study examined the effects of learning motivation, behavioral engagement, cognitive engagement, emotional engagement, agentic engagement, and feedback on college students’ learning performance in physical education. Research design, data and methodology: This study adopted a mixed-methods action research design. The questionnaire was developed based on established literature, and content validity was assessed using the Index of Item-Objective Congruence. Reliability was confirmed through a pilot test with 30 students using Cronbach’s alpha. Quantitative data were collected from 169 valid questionnaires administered to undergraduate students at Guizhou University and analyzed using multiple linear regression to examine relationships between the variables. Based on the regression results and qualitative insights from student interviews, an eight-week Intervention Design Implementation was conducted with 30 students. Paired-sample t-tests were used to compare pre-intervention and post-intervention results. Results: The multiple linear regression analysis indicated that emotional engagement (β = 0.437) and feedback (β = 0.572) had significant positive effects on learning performance, while the other variables showed no significant direct effects. The paired-sample t-test results revealed significant improvements across all variables, including learning performance, after the intervention. Conclusions: The findings suggest that integrating emotional engagement, feedback, and supportive intervention activities can effectively enhance learning performance and support the development of sustained physical exercise habits among college students.

items.title: Analisis Kompetensi Teknik Digital Dan AI Literacy Karyawan Dalam Meningkatkan Efektivitas Pengelolaan Aset Pada Perusahaan Retail: Studi Kasus Pada PT Lancar Wiguna Sejahtera (Lawson)
items.abstract: Digital transformation requires employees to develop digital technical competence and understand the use and limitations of artificial intelligence (AI) in their work. This study examines the roles of digital technical competence and AI literacy in supporting asset management at PT Lancar Wiguna Sejahtera (Lawson), a retail company. A qualitative case study approach was employed, with data collected through interviews involving five informants representing asset administration, store operations, information technology, area supervision, and maintenance functions. The findings indicate that digital technical competence supports the use of internal applications, asset recording, reporting, information verification, and asset status updates. However, the asset management process still faces challenges related to incomplete information, delayed reporting, discrepancies between administrative records and actual asset conditions, and limited visibility of follow-up status. AI literacy involves understanding AI capabilities and limitations, evaluating AI-generated outputs, and protecting confidential company information. The interviews indicate that AI is considered a potential tool for summarizing reports and organizing information, but its outputs require verification against official company records, field conditions, technical knowledge, and operational procedures. No evidence was found that AI had been integrated into the company's official asset management system or used for predictive maintenance. The study highlights the importance of task-based training, mentoring, standardized reporting procedures, information security awareness, and coordination among organizational roles to support more effective asset management.

items.title: Analytics Adoption Factors in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: A Scoping Review Using the Gioia Methodology
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the field of analytics, understood as the continuum from descriptive business intelligence to predictive and prescriptive analytics augmented by machine learning. While organizations are acquiring these systems on a massive scale, the persistent gap between equipment rates and actual usage rates remains largely unexplained. The frameworks inherited from information systems adoption research (the technology acceptance model, the unified theory of acceptance and use of technology, the technology-organization-environment framework, and the diffusion of innovations) were built for systems governed by explicit and auditable rules; their relevance to opaque, partially agentic, and ethically problematic systems has not been systematically examined. This article maps the factors of analytics adoption in the age of AI. The corpus derives from a scoping review that was reported following the PRISMA-ScR protocol: 16,113 records identified, 11,170 screened, 1097 assessed for eligibility, and 42 articles analyzed. The corpus was processed through inductive qualitative content analysis following the Gioia methodology. Coding yielded 106 first-order concepts, 18 s-order themes, and 6 aggregate dimensions. The reliability of the categorization was checked through independent double coding of 18.9% of the coding units: raw agreement reached 80.0%, and Cohen’s kappa was 0.79. The most frequently discussed factors are not the performance attributes of the technology but the socio-organizational and epistemic conditions of its appropriation. The article proposes a moderated mediation model built on three layers: the enabling layer occupies the position of antecedent; the legitimating layer, specific to the age of AI, that of mediator and bottleneck of adoption; and the two dimensions of the actualizing layer that of moderators.

items.title: Anger and gender bias in leadership evaluations: A stereotype-context competition model
items.abstract: Why do female leaders face professional penalties for the same expressions of anger that often benefit male leaders? Despite decades of research, gender bias in leadership evaluations remains a stubborn hurdle for women seeking career advancement. In this theoretical paper, I develop a stereotype-context competition model to explain how gender bias arises in the evaluation of leaders who express anger, and to identify conditions under which such bias is less likely to occur. I argue that evaluations of angry leaders are shaped by two competing forces: a pro-bias force driven by stereotype information and a counter-bias force driven by contextual information. I further propose that the pro-bias force generally prevails, resulting in the persistence of gender bias in initial evaluations of angry leaders. Finally, I identify three categories of factors—related to the leader, the observer, and the situation—that can reduce the likelihood of gender bias. I conclude by discussing the theoretical and practical implications of the model.

items.title: Are We Measuring the Wrong Thing? From Trust Levels to Trust Calibration in Visualization
items.abstract: When a viewer reports that they trust a visualization, what have we measured? Trust measurement in visualization has improved: validated multidimensional inventories are replacing single-item ratings. This position paper argues that level measures answer only part of the question that matters for design. They record how much a person trusts, not whether that trust is warranted or how it changes with use. Research on trust in automation and AI-assisted decision making has long treated calibration, the fit between trust and trustworthiness, as the target. We ask whether that agenda shapes how visualization studies measure trust. Auditing sixteen recent journal studies, six from visualization and ten from an adjacent services literature, we find three gaps. The construct is fragmented. Where visualization experiments record what trust could be judged against, they use different referents and rarely analyse trust against them; the services studies record none. And no design follows trust through failure and repair. We argue that calibration should supplement level measures, identify what trust in a visualization can be calibrated against, and specify the metrics and designs this requires.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) for Medical Research: A Practical Half-Day Training for Clinicians, Residents, and Health Researchers
items.abstract: This record contains a complete, ready-to-deliver half-day training package on the practical and responsible use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in medical research, developed for clinicians and researchers at Ayder Comprehensive Specialized Hospital, Mekelle University. The 32-slide presentation, scheduled from 08:30 to 12:30 with a coffee break, guides participants through the research lifecycle in seven sessions covering AI foundations and prompting, literature searching and study design, academic writing and publishing, qualitative and quantitative data analysis, and ethics, privacy, and verification. Each stage includes realistic, ready-to-use prompt examples for tools such as ChatGPT, PubMed, Google Scholar, and Elicit, alongside live demonstrations of AI-assisted statistical analysis using Stata and R. No technical background is assumed. All acronyms, including AI, ML, LLM, NLP, RAG, PICO/PICOT, PRISMA, and ICMJE, are spelled out and explained in plain language. Relevant research reporting standards, including STROBE, CONSORT, PRISMA, CARE, and EQUATOR, are also introduced at the appropriate stages. To encourage active participation, the training incorporates three hands-on activities: identifying fabricated references, improving an academic abstract, and completing a 20-minute research sprint. The presentation concludes with a two-slide glossary and a verified reference list. Every slide includes detailed, structured speaker notes covering the opening, explanation, practical example, key message, transition, and presenter guidance. This enables any facilitator, including those without a medical or informatics background, to deliver the training confidently. A companion trainer's workbook is also included in this record, containing the training run sheet, timed talking points, demonstration runbooks, activity answer keys, a question-and-answer bank, and a pronunciation guide. All scenarios, quotations, and datasets used throughout the training are fictional or synthetic, ensuring that no real patient information is used. The training consistently emphasises the importance of human oversight and responsible AI use: AI provides drafts and assistance; researchers remain responsible for decisions, verification, and final outputs.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Large Language Models Across the Heart Failure Care Pathway: A Narrative Review
items.abstract: Heart failure affects more than 64 million people worldwide and remains associated with high mortality and recurrent hospitalisation. Artificial intelligence (AI), including large language models (LLMs), is being evaluated across the care pathway, but evidence maturity varies by task. The aim of this narrative review was to appraise direct evidence for LLM applications in heart failure, distinguish it from supporting evidence for other AI methods and propose a risk-based framework for clinical evaluation and governance. The strongest direct LLM evidence concerns electronic health record extraction, document drafting, patient information and clinical trial endpoint adjudication. A small, randomised pilot evaluated supervised generative-AI-guided optimisation of guideline-directed medical therapy. Prospective case-finding and monitoring evidence largely concerns non-LLM AI. For conversational AI telemonitoring (a natural language interface with rule-based alerting), prospective evidence was limited to a single non-randomised controlled pilot. Performance depends on task definition, data completeness, human review and workflow adoption. Overall, LLMs can support clearly defined, supervised heart failure tasks, but current evidence does not justify autonomous high-stakes care. The evidence base is expanding but predominantly retrospective. Prospective trials, disease-specific benchmarks, equity assessment and regulatory engagement are prerequisites for safe clinical translation. Human oversight remains essential across all current-generation applications.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence as a Dynamic Cognitive Partner Integrating Working Memory Theory and AI Supported Reading Development in Dyslexia
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly emerged as a promising resource for supporting students with dyslexia. Nevertheless, much of the existing literature examines AI primarily as an assistive technology, with limited attention to the cognitive mechanisms through which it may enhance reading development. This paper addresses that gap by proposing a conceptual framework that integrates Baddeley’s multicomponent model of working memory with contemporary AI-supported educational tools. Drawing on research in cognitive psychology, special education, cognitive load theory, Universal Design for Learning (UDL), and self-determination theory, the paper argues that AI should be understood not merely as an instructional aid but as an external cognitive support system that complements and extends the functional capacity of working memory during reading. Specifically, the framework illustrates how AI technologies—including text-to-speech systems, speech recognition, adaptive learning environments, and generative AI applications—may reduce cognitive load while supporting the phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, central executive, and episodic buffer. Through this cognitive alignment, AI has the potential to facilitate decoding, comprehension, learner engagement, and reading autonomy among students with dyslexia. The proposed framework contributes to the literature by offering a theoretically grounded perspective that connects cognitive theory with emerging educational technologies. Rather than evaluating the effectiveness of a specific intervention, the paper provides an integrative model to guide future empirical research, instructional design, and the development of AI-supported reading interventions for learners with dyslexia.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Career Guidance and Talent Matching: A Structured Methodological Review of Models, Labels and Trustworthy Evaluation
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in career guidance, occupational recommendation, and candidate-job matching, yet these applications are often treated as interchangeable despite serving different stakeholders and creating distinct downstream risks. This structured methodological review examines how AI methods are evaluated across career matching and algorithmic trustworthiness. Two semantic searches identified 980 unique records, of which 181 studies published in 2020–2026 met the extraction criteria under screening. We purposively selected 19 primary studies for in-depth analysis. Although the field has grown rapidly (62.4% of candidate studies appeared in 2025–2026), the close-read studies show that model performance depends heavily on proxy labels and validation design. High offline performance (area under the curve (AUC) > 0.92) did not consistently translate into robust outcomes: performance degraded for job seekers with few recorded work experiences, a graph baseline reached an AUC of only 0.641, and multimodal interview scoring added negligible predictive gain over text (Spearman ρ = 0.46 vs 0.45) while visual features showed adverse impact (ratio: 0.52). The advantage of fair re-ranking narrowed as employers made more selections, and screeners conformed more often to incorrect recommendations from a bag-of-words model than from a neural model. These findings demonstrate the limitations of static offline metrics. We propose a four-level evaluation framework addressing representation validity, decision-stage stress-testing, human-AI interaction, and consequential impact. Because retrieval was incomplete and inclusion decisions were not independently re-adjudicated, this review assesses methodological practices rather than claiming an exhaustive census.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Educational Frameworks—A Critical Integrative Review of Conceptual Change and Empirical Evidence
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is incorporated into frameworks for teaching, learning, assessment, and educational organization. This critical integrative review examines how these frameworks accommodate AI and the evidence associated with their use. The review used purposive web searches and included publications available by mid-October 2026. The synthesis distinguishes application, contextual specification, construct extension, relational reconfiguration, and AI-specific synthesis across professional knowledge, curriculum, learning, design, inclusion, assessment, and adoption. A source-to-entry crosswalk documents 120 analytical entries linked to 123 publications. Thirty empirical reports and one design case receive a structured access and appraisal record. All 31 selected records were examined in full text. Framework classifications based on partial material remain provisional. The comparison identifies tensions concerning ethical judgment, allocation of cognitive work, and attribution of understanding. Reported competence, AI-assisted products, and independent performance support different educational claims. A worked construct crosswalk shows how agency, regulation, and ethical judgment require distinct units and observations. Science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) provides disciplinary examples within a broader educational scope. The resulting research priorities connect proposed conceptual changes with the evidence needed to examine them.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN ENGLISH LANGUAGE TEACHING AND INNOVATIVE APPROACHES IN LEARNING
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence has become an influential factor in contemporary English language teaching because it expands access to feedback, practice, and personalised learning support. This article examines the role of artificial intelligence in English language teaching and analyses innovative learning approaches associated with its integration. The study is based on a qualitative review of recent academic and policy literature. The findings indicate that AI contributes most visibly to speaking practice, writing support, adaptive learning, learner autonomy, and classroom innovation. At the same time, the literature highlights important challenges, including ethical concerns, overreliance on technology, limited teacher preparation, and the need to preserve meaningful human interaction in the learning process. The article concludes that artificial intelligence should be used not as a replacement for the teacher, but as a pedagogical resource that becomes effective only when integrated critically, ethically, and methodologically.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH: METHODOLOGICAL CAPABILITIES AND LIMITS OF EPISTEMIC AGENCY
items.abstract: The growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in scientific research is changing how data are analysed, hypotheses are generated, and explanations are developed. Algorithmic systems increasingly participate in operations previously carried out directly by researchers. Their contribution, however, raises a methodological question: under what conditions can AI-generated outputs be regarded as justified scientific results rather than merely useful information? This paper examines the capabilities and limitations of AI in scientific inquiry, focusing on the distinction between statistical regularities and causal explanation, the validation of hypotheses, scientific understanding, reproducibility, and researchers' epistemic autonomy. The conceptual basis of this analysis is the distinction between participation in cognitive operations and independent epistemic subjecthood. In the extended-mind approach, external resources may become functionally integrated into human cognition. AI-assisted research likewise involves a distribution of cognitive operations between researchers and algorithmic systems.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence vs. Emotional Intelligence: A Clash Between Technology and Humanity
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is growing faster than ever and changing many parts of our lives. At the same time, emotional intelligence (EI) remains a key human skill that guides our decisions, relationships, and ethical choices. However, there is a growing tension between the strengths of AI and the unique abilities of EI. This article examines how AI and EI interact and sometimes clash, focusing on the balance between technological efficiency and human empathy. By analyzing examples from business, education, and everyday life, the article shows that neither AI nor EI alone can solve all problems. Instead, the future depends on combining the speed and logic of AI with the understanding and insight of EI. Understanding this balance is essential for creating a society that is both advanced and truly human-centered.

items.abstract: This study examines how artificial intelligence-driven assessment systems shape examination integrity across Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board (JAMB) Computer-Based Test (CBT) centres in Nigeria. The study adopted a cross-sectional survey design and drew on a sample of 400 respondents comprising CBT centre supervisors, invigilators, technical officers and returning candidates, selected through multistage sampling across six geopolitical zones. Data were gathered with a structured questionnaire whose reliability returned a Cronbach's alpha of 0.87, and were analysed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation and multiple regression. The findings indicate that AI biometric authentication, AI-enabled remote proctoring and AI anomaly detection each exert a positive and statistically significant effect on examination integrity, with the combined model explaining roughly 61 per cent of the variance in integrity outcomes. Infrastructure reliability and invigilator digital literacy emerged as meaningful conditioning factors. The study concludes that AI systems have measurably strengthened the credibility of JAMB examinations, though their gains remain hostage to power supply, connectivity and human capacity. Recommendations centre on infrastructure investment, sustained capacity-building and a transparent governance framework for algorithmic decision-making in high-stakes assessment

items.title: Artificial Intelligence, Gender Bias, and Human Rights: Challenges for Modern Justice Systems
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly integrated into modern justice systems, influencing decision-making in criminal justice, hiring, surveillance, healthcare, and public administration. Although AI promises efficiency and consistency, a growing body of research documents risks of algorithmic bias and unequal performance across demographic groups. This paper examines the relationship between artificial intelligence, gender bias, and human rights within contemporary justice systems through a qualitative, interdisciplinary analysis combining a narrative review of scholarly literature with doctrinal analysis of relevant international and European legal and ethical frameworks. It considers how biased datasets, discriminatory or uneven algorithmic outcomes, and unequal technological representation may affect fairness, equality, privacy, due process, and access to justice. Particular attention is given to documented evidence on facial-analysis systems and automated recruitment, while broader claims concerning institutional legitimacy and human-centered justice are treated as normative implications rather than empirical findings. The paper also evaluates regulatory responses, including Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (the EU Artificial Intelligence Act) and UNESCO’s Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence. It concludes by identifying transparency, accountability, representative data, independent evaluation, and meaningful human oversight as central safeguards for rights-respecting AI governance. items.title: Asking the Right Questions: A Systematic Literature Review of Algorithmic Literacy in LIS
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems rely on algorithms to simulate human intelligence, learn from data, and support decision-making. Algorithmic literacy is relevant to LIS field because LIS has been at the forefront of promoting literacy at the intersection of people, technology, and information. The ACRL’s AI competency framework for academic library workers stipulates that library workers must be aware of the broad range of ethical issues with AI tools, including the design of “algorithms” (ACRL, 2025:p.4). It will be difficult for library educators, librarians, or any information professionals to be able to ask “good questions” on any AI systems driven by algorithms without possessing algorithmic literacy. While AI literacy is very important, it does not automatically translate into algorithmic literacy. Some of the questions that are yet to be addressed are: How is algorithmic literacy conceptualized in LIS field? What are the specific constructs that can be used to determine its implementation? How can it be assessed, and what are its ethical components beyond AI literacy? To answer these questions, we are synthesizing various LIS literature (within the last 5 years) on algorithmic literacy from four (4) academic databases (WoS, LISTA, Scopus, and ScienceDirect). The study is guided by PRISMA and a three-phase screening process using Yan et al.'s (2023) guidelines (title screening, abstract screening, and full-text review). One of the emerging patterns from the ongoing work at the full review stage is that algorithmic literacy is essential for managing online information services, supporting user engagement, and addressing ethical concerns in algorithmically mediated access.

items.title: Assessment of Student Learning in the Age of Generative AI: Rethinking Assessment Practices in MLIS Programs
items.abstract: The emergence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transforming how students demonstrate their learning, challenging long-standing traditions about what counts as evidence of learning. While there are concerns that students may bypass essential learning processes by using AI to produce content, these tools may also present opportunities to enhance student learning. Grounded in pragmatism, this exploratory-sequential mixed-methods study examines how faculty in graduate programs in Library and Information Science assess student learning in the context of students' use of GenAI, while opening a discussion on how faculty can prepare to both address challenges and leverage opportunities presented by this technology. The first phase involved semi-structured interviews with 15 Master of Library and Information Science (MLIS) faculty members across ALA-accredited programs, analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Findings informed the development of a survey instrument, which generated 206 faculty responses. The survey examined faculty perceptions, readiness, concerns, opportunities, assessment strategies, and best practices related to student use of GenAI. Findings highlight the nuanced and evolving nature of faculty responses to GenAI. Rather than framing AI solely as a threat or a tool for innovation, the results revealed a complex process of recalibrating assessment to foreground authentic learning, transparency, student reasoning, self-reflection, and to prepare graduates for AI-driven work environments. A central tension emerged between preparing students for an AI-driven workforce and preserving higher-order human capacities such as critical thinking, evaluation, ethical reasoning, and professional judgment. The study offers implications for assessment design, curriculum development, AI literacy, and workforce preparation in LIS education.

items.title: Attitude Toward the Integration of Artificial Intelligence Among Public Elementary Teachers and Their Level of Preparedness: The Case of Kasibu West District
items.abstract: Under DepEd Order No. 3, s. 2026, Philippine basic education schools face an urgent mandate to integrate digital and smart technologies into instructional workflows. However, a significant operational divide persists in rural school districts between policy expectations and classroom readiness. This study evaluated the attitudes, instructional preparedness, and operational challenges of public elementary school teachers regarding Artificial Intelligence (AI) integration in Kasibu West District, leading to the development of a structured administrative intervention plan. Grounded in Everett Rogers’ Diffusion of Innovations Theory and the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), a mixed-methods convergent parallel design was employed across all 23 public elementary schools in the district. Quantitative data were gathered from a mathematically determined sample of 120 teachers (N = 172, 100% response rate) selected via proportionate random sampling, using a structured 105-item 4-point Likert instrument. Content validity was established by a panel of three educational experts, and pilot testing with 25 NVSU MAEd graduate students (evaluated by an NVSU university statistician) demonstrated high internal reliability across sub-scales (Attitude α = .939, Preparedness α = .945, Challenges α = .710, Overall α = .910). Results revealed a High overall teacher attitude (Mean = 3.22, SD = 0.42), with Professional Efficiency ranking highest (Mean = 3.37). Instructional preparedness was likewise High (Mean = 3.05, SD = 0.40), led by Behavioral Intentions (Mean = 3.32) but constrained by low Professional Development and Training (Mean = 2.83). Operational challenges were High overall (Mean = 3.12, SD = 0.31), dominated by Technical and Infrastructure Barriers (Mean = 3.36). Inferential analysis yielded a statistically significant, very strong positive correlation between attitude and preparedness (r = .801, p < .001, n = 120), leading to the rejection of the null hypothesis. Qualitative thematic content analysis identified five core grassroots recommendations emphasizing hands-on Learning Action Cell (LAC) training, infrastructure hubs, DepEd-vetted tools, ethical policies, and administrative support. The empirical findings directly informed an expert-validated 4-Phase Administrative Intervention Plan Matrix to systematically address training deficits and upland digital friction.

items.title: Augmenting Data Physicalization Using Visuo-Tactile Illusions
items.abstract: Data physicalizations fabricated by 3D printers are limited in their ability to dynamically vary their form and tactile properties without refabrication, thereby hindering reusability. In particular, tactile properties on the surface of a physicalization (i.e., surface roughness ) cannot be dynamically adjusted as the data change. To address this limitation, we explore a novel method to increase the reusability of a data physicalization, namely perceived tactile modulation (PTM). Our method enables the perception of varying surface roughness levels on a static data physicalization through the use of virtual reality. By altering the visual roughness of the virtual model, we modulate the user’s perception of tactile roughness, thereby influencing how the physicalization is interpreted through touch and expanding the range of ordinal data values that can be encoded. We conducted two studies to design and evaluate this method. In the first study (N = 20), Just Noticeable Differences (JNDs) were established for perceivable visuo-tactile channels in virtual reality environments. The second study (N = 12) investigates the application of our method across two levels of interactive representation: static and interactive. Our findings show that PTM can reliably modulate perceived roughness in static physicalization, while its effectiveness for supporting dynamic, single-artifact updates (interactive encoding) requires further investigation. We present a series of recommendations for applying PTM techniques in data physicalization.

items.title: Awareness, utilization, and pedagogical integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools in biology teaching among science teachers: Toward the development of a training program
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to support instructional planning, the development of learning materials, assessment, and student engagement. However, the extent to which science teachers are aware of, utilize, and pedagogically integrate AI tools in Biology teaching remains an important concern. This study determined the awareness, utilization, and pedagogical integration of AI tools among junior high school science teachers in the Division of Tagbilaran City, Bohol, and examined the predictive contribution of these variables to teachers’ perceived teaching effectiveness and ability to promote student engagement. A quantitative approach using a descriptive-predictive research design was employed. The respondents were 32 junior high school science teachers teaching Biology in public secondary schools, selected through total enumeration. Data were gathered using an adapted structured questionnaire administered through Google Forms and analyzed using frequency, percentage, weighted mean, and multiple linear regression. ChatGPT was the most recognized, currently used, and most useful AI tool. Teachers were aware of AI tools (M = 3.81), frequently utilized them in Biology instruction (M = 3.74), and occasionally integrated them pedagogically (M = 3.35). Their perceived teaching effectiveness and ability to promote student engagement were rated positively (M = 3.68). The regression model significantly predicted the outcome (R² = .603, F = 14.17, p < .001); however, only awareness was a statistically significant predictor (B = 0.450, p < .001). Utilization and pedagogical integration were not significant predictors. The findings informed a proposed professional development program to strengthen teachers’ AI literacy and support the effective, ethical, and curriculum-aligned integration of AI in Biology teaching.

items.title: Beyond Conversations: Spatially-Anchored Previews for Intent Disambiguation in LLM-Assisted Geometry Editing in Virtual Reality
items.abstract: User intent disambiguation remains a key challenge in intelligent interactive systems. While it has been widely studied in dialogue systems in 2D interfaces, research on how intent disambiguation could be incorporated within Large Language Model (LLM) assisted editing workflows in immersive environments remains limited. Recent advances in LLMs create opportunities to leverage the immersive nature of virtual and augmented reality (VR/AR) environments to provide better disambiguation support. In this paper, we evaluate how traditional dialogue-based disambiguation can be augmented with spatially-anchored graphical previews to resolve ambiguous user commands in LLM-assisted parameter-driven editing workflows. A within-subjects study in which 24 participants completed complex geometry editing tasks in VR simulates scenarios where VR scenes are controlled by numerical parameters. Compared with the condition where disambiguation is not available, quantitative metrics and qualitative feedback indicate that a hybrid approach which combines clarification questions and graphical previews can support better interaction stability with fewer conversation rounds while improving user experience. These findings provide empirical evidence on the effectiveness of disambiguation methods in LLM-assisted editing of parameter-driven immersive scenes and inform design guidelines for future integration of LLMs in advanced VR/AR systems.

items.title: Beyond Driver Monitoring: A Systems Approach to Understanding Lifecycle Risks of AI-Based Driver Behaviour Monitoring Systems
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence-based Driver Behaviour Monitoring Systems (AI-DBMS) are used in heavy vehicle fleets to detect unsafe driving states and behaviours such as fatigue and distraction. However, limited research has examined risks across their lifecycle. This study used Hierarchical Task Analysis (HTA) to identify risks associated with AI-DBMS implementation. An HTA model of the AI-DBMS lifecycle was developed and validated through interviews with technology developers, fleet operators, regulators, and researchers. Participants selected HTA sub-goals relevant to their expertise and discussed risks and controls. Five risk categories were identified: (i) technology and system design, (ii) data-related, (iii) governance and regulatory, (iv) organisational, and (v) human and behavioural. Four control categories were identified: (i) governance and organisational, (ii) human-centred design and implementation, (iii) system assurance, and (iv) data management. Findings show AI-DBMS risks extend beyond technical performance and the driver-technology interface, highlighting the need for coordinated Human Factors approaches across the AI-DBMS lifecycle.

items.title: Beyond Knowledge Transfer: Non-Human Embodiment for Environmental Education
items.abstract: Effective conservation education must communicate ecological facts while also making distant environmental threats personally meaningful. Virtual reality (VR) may support this goal by allowing learners to experience such threats from a non-human perspective, yet it remains unclear whether embodied interactive VR primarily improves factual learning, affective engagement, or both. We present EcoShift VR, a dual-ecosystem experience in which users embody either a Sunda pangolin facing pollution and poaching or a blue shark facing pollution and bycatch. We evaluated EcoShift VR in a controlled 2 × 2 between-subjects study ( N = 40) comparing Medium (embodied interactive VR vs. lecture-style informational video) and Ecosystem (terrestrial vs. marine). As the media differed jointly in immersion, embodiment, agency, and interaction, their individual contributions cannot be isolated. All four conditions showed significant within-group factual knowledge gains after Holm–Bonferroni correction across the four paired comparisons, with no significant Medium effect on knowledge gain. Before multiplicity correction, 10 of the 13 Medium effects were statistically significant and favored embodied interactive VR, including nature connectedness, state empathy, perceived environmental awareness, and several curiosity and inquisitiveness measures. After Holm–Bonferroni adjustment across the 13 Medium comparisons, only the three state-empathy subscales (affective, cognitive, and associative) and the post-experience domain-specific curiosity composite remained statistically significant. A secondary within-condition analysis also identified a significant increase in nature connectedness for VR–Marine ( p Holm =.0053), although the overall Medium effect on nature connectedness did not survive correction. Other initially significant Medium effects were similarly attenuated after adjustment, while environmental-attitude gains remained directionally favorable to VR but inconclusive. These findings suggest that the broader embodied interactive VR experience can complement conventional environmental education, particularly by supporting empathy and conservation-oriented curiosity alongside factual learning.

items.title: Beyond Model Choice: Designing Maintainable and Source-Grounded LLM Assistants for Academic Advising
items.abstract: Students increasingly rely on Large Language Models (LLMs) for academic advice, yet general-purpose models often lack institution-specific knowledge and can provide confident but inaccurate guidance. This creates risks for students and raises design questions about how universities should develop reliable, accountable, and maintainable LLM advising systems. This study evaluates three approaches for incorporating institutional knowledge into LLM-based advising systems: prompting, retrieval, and fine-tuning, compared across three open-weight models producing 48 configurations. Evaluation used an LLM-as-judge framework validated by student advisors serving as domain experts. Results show that the system prompt has the greatest impact on response quality, while retrieval provides complementary gains through source attribution. Fine-tuning produces only modest improvements. The LLM judge closely mirrors expert rankings, though it consistently assigns higher scores. These findings shift attention from model performance alone to the design and governance of maintainable, source-visible, uncertainty-aware advising systems embedded within human-led academic advising practice.

items.title: Beyond Resume Keywords: Eliminating Entry-Level Burnout Through AI-Driven Workplace Culture Matching
items.abstract: Entry-level hiring in emerging startup ecosystems suffers from a critical structural flaw: an over-reliance on superficial resume keyword matching at the expense of workplace culture compatibility. Drawing on industry workforce data and qualitative insights synthesized from over 50 structured interviews with Chief Human Resources Officers (CHROs) and startup founders on the career podcast "Let’s Hear It From...", this paper examines the root causes of early-career attrition and Gen-Z workplace burnout. Industry benchmarks indicate that early-stage companies face a 43.7% rookie attrition rate—incurring ₹1.5 lakh to ₹3 lakh per bad hire—while 47.5% of startup employees report low psychological well-being. Qualitative findings reveal five recurring failure points among fresh graduates: mindset misalignment, inadequate organizational research, AI-assisted interview façades, theoretical baggage paired with low learning agility, and workplace etiquette deficits. To address this misalignment, this paper introduces the Human Energy Matching Framework, an automated, cognitive AI-driven methodology deployed via AlignCulture. By cross-referencing unstructured executive cultural baselines with multidimensional candidate behavioral assessments across dimensions such as Values Alignment, Learning Agility, Work Style Fit, and Purpose Alignment, organizations and higher education placement cells can transition from reactive keyword filtering to sustainable, wellness-driven talent integration. Author’s Note: Generative AI tools were utilized to assist in synthesizing qualitative transcripts from the "Let's Hear It From..." podcast archive and structuring the manuscript. All conceptual frameworks, empirical observations, and conclusions are the sole work of the author.

items.title: Boundaries for generative AI use and task delegation in nursing education: a scoping review with critical evidence synthesis
items.abstract: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in nursing education, but studies rarely evaluate task delegation explicitly. This review mapped evidence on educational tasks, contexts of use, and safeguards to inform boundaries for using large language models (LLMs) and delegating educational tasks. Methods This scoping review with critical evidence synthesis used JBI guidance for evidence mapping and PRISMA-ScR for reporting. MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched through 7 August 2026 for studies involving direct interaction between prelicensure nursing students and LLM-based systems. The review team extracted outcomes, risks, safeguards, and human oversight. The team proposed delegation statuses by considering the consequences of error, error detectability under specified safeguards, the need for human judgment, confidence in the evidence, and oversight feasibility. Results Of the 440 records screened, 46 studies comprising 47 educational application profiles were included. Of the 146 outcome records, 115 were favorable, 13 were mixed, 10 showed no difference, 6 were unfavorable, and 2 were unclear. Twelve studies (26.1%) reported at least one objectively verified error or event or an adverse educational outcome. Among the 118 safeguards, 100 (84.7%) were proposed or implemented without evaluation beyond implementation, five (4.2%) were evaluated for feasibility or acceptability, and 13 (11.0%) were evaluated for risk reduction. The proposed matrix comprises 16 task categories: eight conditionally delegable, five restricted to a supportive role, two unsuitable for automated delegation, and one with insufficient evidence. Conclusion The matrix offers a preliminary framework for task-specific decisions. Bounded knowledge support and low-risk formative feedback may be conditionally delegable with appropriate safeguards and oversight. AI should support clinical reasoning and care planning, whereas final grading, competence decisions, and ethical judgment should remain human responsibilities. The matrix requires validation and updating as direct evidence, particularly on safeguard effectiveness, becomes available. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is renowned for its stochastic nature, where powerful computational performance is jeopardized by inconsistent, vague, and even flawed reasoning. When it comes to teaching MLIS students about serving information needs, seeking, use, and literacy, AI curricula present both opportunities and limitations to successful instruction. A research team explored a critical curriculum that draws distinctly from LIS examples of search trends, AI hallucination, and scholarly risks. Rather than a fixed and performance-based curriculum, this learning material aimed to bring MLIS students into conversations on AI use, risks, and even refusal. This work-in-progress study, which centers on student agency, contemplation, and critique, offers preliminary findings and opportunities for idea exchanges among LIS faculty.

items.title: Calibration-Free Eye Tracking through Binocular-Constrained Homography Normalization
items.abstract: Implicit user calibration and calibration-free eye-tracking methods have been explored to improve the usability of gaze-based interactions. However, these methods for regression- and model-based approaches typically require multiple observations or camera-display calibration. Therefore, we propose a binocular-constrained homography normalization method that enables calibration-free gaze estimation from a single observation without camera-display calibration. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first homography-based framework to incorporate calibration-free gaze estimation. For each eye, the corneal center and optical axis are estimated using a 3D eyeball model with a monocular camera, and the point-of-gaze is computed using homography transformations derived from both eyes. The proposed method achieved a mean horizontal angular error of 1.01° under the tested conditions. The experimental evaluations supported the feasibility of the proposed method and identified directions for further improvement.

items.title: Can AI Make with Us? Exploring Tacit Knowledge and Emotion in AI-Supported Making
items.abstract: As AI reshapes how people learn and create, questions arise about forms of knowledge that are embodied, practice-based, and difficult to articulate. This study examines how learners physically co-create with AI and what forms of tacit knowledge emerge through that process. It further investigates how emotions surface and are managed throughout AI-supported making. Through this examination, this study aims to holistically capture the cognitive, emotional, and behavioral dimensions of tacit knowledge acquisition in an AI-supported making environment. We designed and facilitated a pilot workshop centered on e-textile making with community members in Champaign-Urbana, Illinois in April 2026. E-textile was selected for its inherently tactile and embodied nature, offering a deliberate contrast to AI’s text-based, formalized mode of knowledge. Nine participants engaged freely with AI tools of their choice alongside human facilitators, creating a naturalistic environment where both forms of support coexisted. To capture the holistic process of cognition, behavioral patterns, and emotional responses, think-aloud protocols, observation, pre-post surveys, and interviews were used as data collection methods. Preliminary findings reveal no consensus on how AI supported ideation, process, or outcomes, suggesting that its role in tacit-knowledge-rich making is highly individual. Emotionally, participants expressed confidence, curiosity, and surprise throughout the workshops, while also navigating moments of stress and frustration. This study contributes to Library and Information Science understanding of how human-AI collaboration unfolds in spaces where knowledge is socially constructed and physically embodied. It further offers insight into the emotional experiences that emerge and are managed throughout AI-supported learning.

items.title: Can AI Personalise Meaningfulness? Bodies, Prediction, and Postdigital Health and Physical Education
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly woven into Health and Physical Education (HPE) through motion analysis, wearable data, adaptive task design, automated feedback, and generative support for teachers. These developments are often associated with personalisation and, by extension, with the possibility of making learning more meaningful for individual students. This conceptual article questions that connection. Drawing on Kretchmar’s philosophy of meaning in movement, Meaningful Physical Education (MPE), and postdigital accounts of entangled pedagogy and technological mediation, it argues that meaningfulness is not a personalised output but a postdigital accomplishment. It emerges through embodied activity, relationships, material settings, cultural practices, interpretation, and time. Particular AI-supported arrangements may expand or constrain these conditions, but no technical adjustment can guarantee what an experience will come to mean. The analysis develops four tensions: personal relevance between dialogue and prediction; challenge between embodied negotiation and adaptive optimisation; fun, sociality, and delight beyond engagement analytics; and biographical meaning in relation to computational memory. It shows how personalised systems can also influence whose movements, preferences, and histories become visible and valued. The article concludes with five commitments for keeping meaningfulness open in postdigital HPE: interpretive openness, negotiated personalisation, embodied and relational attentiveness, collective possibility, and temporal and infrastructural humility.
