items.title: Clinical AI agents: a short narrative review
items.abstract: Clinical artificial intelligence (AI) agents represent an emerging generation of AI systems. They extend conventional clinical decision support through goal-directed planning, tool interaction and adaptation of actions to intermediate results. Memory may support these functions but is not essential in every implementation. Human oversight is a safeguard for clinical deployment rather than an intrinsic capability. This short narrative review summarizes current evidence regarding the core architectural features, representative clinical applications, and primary implementation challenges of clinical AI agents. Recent studies indicate promising applications in diagnostic decision support, workflow automation, patient communication, and evidence synthesis. However, existing evidence remains largely based on technical validation studies, proof-of-concept systems, and conceptual frameworks, with relatively limited prospective evaluation in routine clinical practice. Key challenges include establishing reliable evaluation frameworks, ensuring process-level safety, developing effective governance structures, and generating robust clinical evidence to support implementation. Although technological progress is rapid, widespread adoption will require not only further technical advances but also rigorous clinical validation, transparent governance, and successful integration into healthcare workflows. Clinical AI agents may become useful components of multidisciplinary healthcare workflows, provided that future research addresses the remaining methodological and implementation challenges.

items.title: Cluster-Based Learner Profiling in AI-Supported Educational Contexts: Evidence from Junior High School Students
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly embedded in educational settings, learner heterogeneity can no longer be adequately described through single-variable comparisons. This study identifies learner profiles in AI-supported educational contexts using three theoretically grounded feature dimensions: AI self-efficacy, digital literacy, and cross-disciplinary integration self-efficacy. These dimensions were operationalized using eight indicators reflecting students’ AI-related confidence, digital information-processing competence, and integrative learning readiness. Based on 8,022 valid responses from eighth-grade students in the collaborative database of the Taiwan Assessment of Student Achievement: Longitudinal Study and the Taiwan i-Generation Panel Study, available from the Survey Research Data Archive, Academia Sinica, all input indicators were normalized using Z -score scaling to construct a standardized feature space for distance estimation. A two-stage clustering procedure was adopted. First, two-step cluster analysis was performed to compare candidate solutions based on Akaike Information Criterion and Bayesian Information Criterion values; subsequently, K -means clustering was conducted with the number of clusters fixed at six to estimate the final learner profiles. The results supported six profiles: high-scoring integrated; very low-scoring; AI-moderate, digitally weak; broadly below-average; digitally adequate, AI-integration weak; and near-average balanced. The profiles showed that learner heterogeneity was not organized along a simple high–low continuum but appeared as asymmetric configurations within the multidimensional feature space. Post-clustering analyses further showed that digital-literacy indicators and AI evaluation had the largest descriptive between-profile separations, and that cluster membership differed significantly by gender. The findings extend AI literacy research from average-based comparisons to cluster-based learner profiling and provide a basis for differentiated educational support and data-driven decision-making in AI-related educational settings.

items.title: Collaboration to Constraint: Rethinking Generative Artificial Intelligence in User Experience & Interface Design
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) tools have become a standard in the User Experience (UX) & User Interface (UI) design workflows. There has been a shift in Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems reshaping how designers ideate, research, generate layouts, and refine interfaces. These AI systems promise speed and creativity within the UX workflows, but the increase in AI integration has raised questions around control and autonomy shift when they are used for design generation. In this thesis I have investigated the design outcomes when AI is positioned as a creative collaborator, influencing the decision authority and cognitive ownership. In this study, I have used research-through-design combining with auto-ethnography reflections, comparative user interface generation experiments (including Lovable AI-based website creations), and participatory engagements like Open Studio activity and a co-design workshop. The findings suggested that introducing AI early in the design process can lead the design to a specific framework, hierarchy and interaction pattern that narrow divergence. Designers can experience a drift in cognitive ownership while retaining their decision authority when authorship is distributed across prompts, iterations, and AI-generated drafts. In my experiments, AI outputs were polished and plausible but converged towards a similar structural layout. It reflected the influence of dominant pattern in their training data. This thesis argues for responsible integration of AI through careful timing, clear override options, and tools that make AI-driven influence visible, instead of rejecting it completely.

items.title: CoMotion: A Real-Time System for User-Driven Semantic Steering in Text-to-Motion Generation
items.abstract: Current text-to-motion frameworks typically operate as a rigid, one-shot workflow where users are unable to intervene during the generation process, effectively limiting all refinement efforts to the iterative modification of the text prompt. This black-box process hinders iterative design, leading to inefficiency. Furthermore, natural language inherently suffers from ambiguity when describing fine-grained 3D motions, making it difficult for users to articulate their intent solely through text precisely. In this paper, we propose CoMotion , a real-time system that shifts the interaction paradigm from static text prompting to user-driven semantic steering. Instead of requiring users to restart the entire generation process for every modification, CoMotion operates directly within a discrete latent space by retrieving prompt-relevant atomic actions and presenting them as user-visible, adjustable controls. Through CoMotion , users can adjust semantic steering levels for these atomic actions to guide the generation toward their intent without the computational overhead of full text-to-motion model re-inference. Our approach provides a more diverse design pathway for the traditional one-shot text-to-motion generation process, enabling fine-grained, personalized motion control during generation. We validate our system using a standardized benchmark based on Large Language Models. Quantitative experiments demonstrate that CoMotion enables robust semantic correction and geometric diversity while maintaining the kinematic quality of the generated motions. Crucially, by transforming complex generative tasks into low-latency, interactive operations, CoMotion supports an interactive refinement workflow for the evaluated motion generation tasks.

items.title: Consequential Human Agency in AI-Enabled Higher Education: Capability, Institutional Authority, and the Right to Contest
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is intensifying longstanding questions about the purposes of higher education, the authority of human judgment, and the university's obligations to society. This conceptual, theory-building article argues that AI competence is educationally insufficient when learners lack institutional conditions that make judgment consequential. Drawing on AI-literacy scholarship, ecological theories of agency, democratic education, the capabilities approach, and critical educational technology, it develops an ecological framework of Consequential Human Agency. The framework distinguishes individual capability from agency achieved in interaction with institutional authority, rights to contest and appeal, accountability, and material conditions of participation. Ethical, civic, professional, and leadership agency are treated as contexts of enactment rather than stages or measurable competencies. The article argues that universities are not benign guarantors of agency: as purchasers of platforms, assessment authorities, and users of surveillance and analytics, they can enable or constrain it. Higher education should therefore cultivate judgment while establishing institutional rights and procedures through which students and faculty can question, override, appeal, and help govern consequential AI-mediated decisions.

items.title: Continuing Education as Ethical Infrastructure: Informal AI Learning in Academic Librarianship
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming academic librarianship, requiring sustained ethical, evaluative, and instructional learning. Drawing on interviews with fourteen U.S. STEM academic librarians and scholarship on AI literacy and professional development, this paper examines how librarians develop AI competence through experimentation, peer networks, and personal knowledge management amid uneven institutional support. These conditions shift the costs of adaptation onto individual practitioners and raise concerns about equity, labor, and sustainability. The paper reframes continuing education as sociotechnical infrastructure for AI learning, identifies informal learning as structurally compelled labor, and proposes a role for library and information science (LIS) educators in designing ethical, collaborative, and sustained professional learning. Practice-based pathways, communities of practice, protected learning time, and institutional governance can support critical judgment as AI systems change.

items.abstract: This article offers a philosophical reconstruction of the criteria for artistic mastery in the context of the proliferation of digital media and generative artificial intelligence. It challenges the tendency to equate mastery solely with technical proficiency, professional status, or the visual perfection of a work, while conversely reducing amateurism merely to aesthetic inferiority. The methodology integrates a phenomenological analysis of aesthetic experience, the hermeneutics of artistic decision-making, a media-philosophical perspective, and a critical examination of contemporary literature on the philosophy of AI. It is argued that generative technology alters not only the artist’s toolkit but also the modes of form emergence, the distribution of agency, and the processes of perception. The study proposes distinguishing between image generation, its artistic articulation, and the aesthetic event, processes that do not necessarily coincide. The novelty of this research lies in delineating three levels of an artistic work-technical generation, authorial articulation, and the aesthetic event and in conceptualizing mastery as a reflexively responsible capacity to organize the relationships between these levels, rather than as a mere sum of skills or a property of a finished artifact. Conclusions. Based on this, a multidimensional model of mastery is developed, encompassing intentionality, media literacy, reflexive selection, temporal depth, the productivity of aesthetic experience, and responsibility. It is demonstrated that the «human versus machine» dichotomy is less analytically productive than the distinction between the automated reproduction of the recognizable and responsible form-creation. Amateurism is interpreted as an open mode of participation in culture—one capable of evolving into mastery, independent of commercial or institutional legitimation.

items.title: Creating meaning at work or providing career support? How servant leaders enhance followers’ vocational outcomes
items.abstract: Do servant leaders shape their followers’ vocational outcomes by the career support they provide or by helping followers find meaning at work? Drawing on self-determination theory, we test these two accounts, examining their competing effects on followers’ thriving at work, career satisfaction, and job search behaviors. Using the critical incident method (Study 1), we found that servant leaders influence vocational outcomes by deepening followers’ meaning at work, but not by providing career support. In a four-wave study (Study 2), both pathways were significant. A field study (Study 3) again supported only the meaning at work pathway, showing that meaning at work was most salient for followers with lower levels of work volition. An internal meta-analysis confirmed that both pathways carry a positive indirect effect in aggregate, but that the pathway through meaning at work is significantly stronger. Taken together, our results indicate that servant leadership is more vocationally consequential through the meaning followers internalize than the career support they receive, particularly among followers whose vocational agency is more constrained.

items.title: Designing AI at the Rural Edge: A Micro-Social Venture Framework for Community-Led Digital Innovation
items.abstract: Generative and other AI-enabled technologies are accessible to small organisations, yet human–AI interaction (HAI) design guidance focuses on relatively direct user–system interaction. Rural HCI, community-centred design, participatory AI, digital inclusion, and social-enterprise research show that AI use is socially and organisationally situated. This late-breaking work develops the Micro-Social Venture (MSV) Framework through integrative conceptual synthesis of 55 selected sources. The framework connects six dimensions: Place, Community Agency, Organisational Mediation, Digital and AI Capability, Resource Conditions, and Governance and Social Outcomes. Its distinctive contribution is to treat the social venture as part of HAI itself: a community-embedded socio-technical intermediary through which AI is encountered, adapted, governed, and potentially refused. Five design propositions address place, collective agency, resource asymmetry, negotiated trust, and community stewardship. The framework is generative rather than predictive, offering HCI a diagnostic lens for examining community-embedded AI at geographic, organisational, infrastructural, and participatory edges.

items.title: DESIGNING AI-RESISTANT TASKS AS A TOOL FOR ASSESSING THE ANALYTICAL AND CRITICAL COMPETENCIES OF FUTURE TEACHERS
items.abstract: This article provides a theoretical foundation for assessing the analytical and critical competencies of future teachers in the era of generative artificial intelligence. It has been demonstrated that the limited reliability of automated AI-detection tools necessitates a shift from evaluating the final written product to a "process-over-product" diagnostic paradigm, while upholding the principles of academic integrity. Within the structure of an educator's analytical - critical competencies, the cognitive-diagnostic, didactic-design and reflexive-metacognitive components have been distinguished. A didactic model has been developed for designing AI - resistant assignments that focus on higher-order thinking skills, specifically "Analyzing", "Evaluating" and ″Creating″ according to Bloom's Taxonomy. The model incorporates the ″Three Zones ″ framework and utilizes three diagnostic formats: the analysis of contradictory pedagogical cases (Case Study), the cognitive auditing of AI-generated content (Reverse Engineering), and in-person, dialogue-based defense using the Socratic method (Socratic Defense). Furthermore, a criterion - based, multi-level rubric has been proposed comprising verification-analytical, didactic-adaptive, and metacognitive-authorial criteria to objectively assess students' professional agency and critical thinking.

items.title: Determinants of Mechanical Ventilator Adoption in Healthcare Emergency Settings
items.abstract: Mechanical ventilation (MV) is the recommended standard of care in many emergencies, yet its adoption by nursing professionals remains inconsistent. This research examines whether perceived clinical expertise is associated with emergency nurses' intention to use MV, directly and indirectly through trust in MV technology and attitude toward MV, and whether emergency severity moderates these associations. Emergency nurses (N = 236) were randomly assigned to one of four vignettes of decreasing acuity: cardiorespiratory arrest, severe hypoxaemia, chest trauma with respiratory compromise, and acute pulmonary oedema. Structural equation modelling showed that expertise was associated with trust and intention, trust with attitude, and attitude with intention; the serial indirect effect of expertise on intention through trust and attitude was significant. Because these constructs were measured concurrently, this effect is interpreted as an indirect association rather than as evidence of causal transmission. Higher severity strengthened the direct association between expertise and intention and weakened the association between trust and attitude, so that the serial indirect association declined as acuity increased. These findings are consistent with a shift from deliberative to automatic processing under time pressure and suggest that training should build expertise to automaticity for maximum-acuity scenarios while fostering trust in lower-acuity ones.

items.title: Digital Health Innovations and Well-Being of the Aged Population: A Theoretical Approach
items.abstract: Digital health innovations are increasingly reshaping the delivery of healthcare and creating new possibilities for supporting the well-being of ageing populations. From telemedicine and remote patient monitoring to mobile health applications, wearable devices, and artificial intelligence-enabled services, these technologies can improve access to healthcare, strengthen disease management, and promote greater independence among older adults. However, their implications for the well-being of the aged population extend beyond clinical outcomes and involve psychological, social, behavioral, and functional dimensions of ageing. The paper adopted a secondary source of data. This theoretical study examines the relationship between digital health innovations and the well-being of older adults by synthesizing insights from existing conceptual and empirical literature and adopted successful aging theory as a framework to the study. The study conceptualizes digital health as an enabling mechanism through which older adults can participate more actively in managing their health and maintaining social connectedness. In conclusion, disparities in digital access, privacy concerns, technological complexity, and age-related are key to the health benefits of the aging population. The study recommends a conceptual perspective that integrates technological, individual, and social factors to explain how digital health innovations can contribute to healthier, more autonomous, and socially connected ageing. Keywords: Digital health, innovations, well-being, aged and population

items.title: Digital innovation and public acceptance of nuclear energy in the green transition
items.abstract: Public acceptance is widely regarded as a binding constraint on the contribution of nuclear energy to the green transition, yet claims that digital innovation will ease this constraint have rarely been examined against social science evidence. This topical review asks under what conditions digital innovation in nuclear energy systems, in particular digital twins, artificial intelligence (AI)-based predictive maintenance and the digitally supported design, manufacture and operation of small modular reactors (SMRs), can contribute to public acceptance of nuclear energy. The analysis draws on five strands of scholarship that are seldom brought into contact with the technical literature: risk perception research, cultural theory of risk, the deficit and engagement models of science communication, the social licence to operate, and socio-technical transitions theory, which serves as the integrating framework. Reading techno-optimistic claims through these lenses, the review identifies three structural barriers: a cybersecurity paradox, whereby the connectivity that enables digital safety functions simultaneously expands the attack surface; an economic gap, specific to SMRs, whereby projected cost reductions rest on serial-production assumptions that recent project experience has not supported; and a transparency fallacy, whereby information disclosure is expected to build trust although meta-analytic evidence links the benefit and risk perceptions associated with acceptance to trust rather than to knowledge. These barriers are argued to interact: cyber incidents could act as trust-destroying signal events, cost failures could undermine perceived institutional competence, and one-way transparency tools leave procedural justice concerns unaddressed. The review concludes that digital innovation is more likely to support acceptance when it is embedded in genuinely participatory engagement, when institutions demonstrably manage the new risks digitalisation creates, when economic claims are validated rather than promised, and when regulatory frameworks confer procedural legitimacy. Absent these conditions, digitalisation risks reproducing deficit-model assumptions that acceptance research has long found wanting.

items.title: Digital Policing and Artificial Intelligence: Implications for Community Trust and Police Legitimacy in Abia State, Nigeria
items.abstract: This study examines the implications of digital policing and Artificial Intelligence (AI) adoption in the Nigeria Police Force for community trust and police legitimacy, with particular reference to Abia State. Anchored in Procedural Justice Theory, the study adopts a qualitative desk-review design, synthesizing peer-reviewed literature on digital policing, algorithmic decision-making, and Nigerian police-community relations. Abia State, with a 2006 census population of 2,845,380 spread across seventeen local government areas, provides a densely populated, predominantly urban and semi-urban context in which the legitimacy consequences of digital policing carry direct relevance for millions of residents. The review finds that digital tools carry real potential to strengthen policing capacity, but that their value for legitimacy depends less on technical sophistication than on whether their deployment is experienced by citizens as fair, transparent, and respectful. Evidence from Nigerian policing scholarship indicates that public confidence in the police remains persistently low, human discretion continues to compromise the neutrality of ostensibly objective digital systems, and police-public digital interaction in Nigeria remains predominantly one-directional rather than participatory. The study argues that without deliberate attention to voice, neutrality, and trustworthiness, the introduction of AI and digital infrastructure into Nigerian policing risks reproducing, rather than resolving, the legitimacy deficits that have long characterized police-community relations, and recommends that digital policing reform in Abia State be paired with institutional accountability and genuine community engagement. Keywords: Digital policing, digitalization, artificial intelligence, police legitimacy, community trust, procedural justice, Abia State

items.title: Do Digital Nudges Survive Complexity? Cognitive Biases and AI Assistance in Time-Series Financial Decisions
items.abstract: Most evidence for digital nudges comes from simple choice sets. We test whether they still work in information-dense financial interfaces and how AI assistants affect them. In an online experiment, 252 participants from Armenia managed a two-currency portfolio and made buy, hold, or sell decisions on dynamic time-series charts. Each participant saw five of ten manipulations under one of four AI conditions: no assistant or a neutral, biased, or debiasing assistant. Four manipulations shifted choices toward their target actions. A stated 70% chance of growth had the largest effect (+36.5 percentage points), followed by adding a third, decoy forecast to the two-forecast control set (+29.4 pp relative to that set), an upward price spike (+25.4 pp), and red highlighting of losses (+23.8 pp). The rest, including social proof and anchoring, had no significant effect. Paired nudges worked differently by direction: numeric and verbal cues mainly pushed buying, and the red cue pushed selling. A biased assistant roughly doubled the odds of the target action, while neutral and debiasing assistants had no detectable effect. Specific cues in the price chart still work in complex displays, and AI strengthens them more easily than it corrects them.

items.title: Don't Take the Researcher Out of Research: Perspectives on AI from Qualitative Scholars
items.abstract: In line with the explosion of public, political, and educational discourses around the incorporation of artificial intelligence (AI) in everyday life, researchers have recently invested a significant amount of time into exploring and theorizing the use of AI in qualitative data analysis. This proposed use of AI creates a theoretical friction with qualitative methodologists who foreground the interpretive (and essentially human) elements of this research praxis. To productively engage with this friction, authors--who span from being more quantitatively oriented to those who are considered Big Q Qualitative researchers--engaged in conversations with one another in a reflexive process of self-study. To help facilitate these conversations, all the authors explored CAILA, a qualitative analysis tool that uses AI to autonomously generate codes and themes from a text-based data set. Authors familiar with the tool spoke to the other three scholars who begrudgingly experimented with CAILA for the first--and last--time. Analysis of these conversations showed that participants felt that AI-based research tools could support menial aspects of qualitative analysis or help with coding of data based on established codebooks. However, the participants also found that tools like CAILA failed to provide meaningful interpretations of the data and stripped the humanistic components of qualitative research from the analysis process. These findings sit in opposition to the purported value of AI software, which emphasizes the efficiency of research processes. To this end, our findings position qualitative research as a human pursuit, asserting that the slow pace of the coding processes provides the space needed for researchers to develop new ideas and meaning from bodies of text. We contribute to the ongoing conversation about using AI for qualitative data analysis by providing fresh perspectives from Big Q Qualitative methodologists and inviting the field to think more deeply about the qualitative research process.

items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) now underpins FinTech services that support digital financial inclusion and sustainable economic growth, yet AI-enabled fraud threatens users' trust in this innovation. Some users intend to discontinue AI-enabled FinTech services even when they are satisfied and habituated, a pattern that traditional continuance explanations do not explain. This study examines a Dual Evaluation Mechanism in which discontinuance intention forms through an internal path (confirmation, satisfaction, and habit) and an external path (vicarious exposure to AI fraud and perceived AI fraud risk), and tests whether perceived AI fraud risk moderates the relationship between habit and discontinuance intention. The study employs cross-sectional survey data from 507 Indian users of AI-enabled FinTech services, analyzed with partial least squares structural equation modeling and complemented by predictive, importance-performance, endogeneity, and necessary condition analyses. The results show that confirmation raises satisfaction (β = 0.648), satisfaction raises habit (β = 0.578), and habit lowers discontinuance intention (β = −0.330). Vicarious AI fraud exposure raises perceived AI fraud risk (β = 0.588), which raises discontinuance intention (β = 0.507), and the interaction between risk and habit is positive (β = 0.174); all paths are significant at p < 0.001. The model explains 39.9% of the variance in discontinuance intention and outperforms the indicator-average benchmark in out-of-sample prediction. The findings suggest that all six hypotheses are supported, that perceived AI fraud risk is the most important predictor of discontinuance intention (0.507) and weakens the protective effect of habit, and that no construct is a strong necessary condition for discontinuance (d ≤ 0.163). items.title: EFFECTIVE WAYS TO USE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN TEACHING ENGLISH AS A FOREIGN LANGUAGE (EFL)
items.abstract: This thesis examines how artificial intelligence (AI) can be used effectively in teaching English as a foreign language. It reviews the theoretical grounds for AI-supported instruction and describes five pedagogically sound applications: automated writing feedback, conversational practice with chatbots and voice assistants, adaptive personalization, generative AI for materials development, and AI-assisted assessment. It also considers risks such as over-reliance, accuracy problems, and ethical concerns. The analysis suggests that AI is most effective when it complements, rather than replaces, the teacher, when it is tied to clear learning objectives, and when learners are trained to use it critically.
